chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
title: Chick Webb's wake and funeral in Baltimore
summary: The band attends the wake in Webb's Baltimore home, where thousands filed through.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: I think I was telling you that after we arrived in Montgomery, Alabama that day --
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
the day he passed away, we didn't know about it. We played about four sets before we were told of his death.
Yeah.
My manager called Ella Fitzgerald, then he called Taft and a couple of guys and he informed us that Chick had passed away.

I think we played one more set and they called the dance off for that night. (Inaudible) we didn't return. We stayed there about two or three o'clock in the morning, you know, talking -- getting it straightened out.
And we returned to Baltimore the next morning (inaudible). (Inaudible) were there at the funeral. And we stayed there the whole time (inaudible).
People came from all over. I remember they had his body laid out in his home on the first floor. It was like a three-story house, in Baltimore, with the steps...
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

And the day of the funeral, everybody, (inaudible) school kids -- all walks of life. Cab drivers, truck drivers -- everybody came by the street and parker their cars to come in to see -- to view the body.

So anyway, his body was laid out on the first floor of the little parlor there. And the people were coming in -- they were going to try to get in and get out, so they just opened up the back so they could go all the way through the kitchen, out and around the side and come out that way.

And people came all that day, all that night. The band came, we were (inaudible) on the top floor. Chick would say (inaudible) anything happen, you know, don't be down in the dumps, you know. Chick Webb wanted everybody was (inaudible) happy, you know. Like he would always take the burden (inaudible). You know, keep everybody happy (inaudible). So, that's the -- we were happy (inaudible) the whole time the funeral was going on. He had an uncle there about seventy years old -- he might be in the eighties.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
He had real strong hands. He sat with the band up on the top floor. He kept us laughing the whole time, you know, (inaudible).

The next day of the funeral, they had it roped off all the way across from his home -- cross Baltimore. They had laid out a path for the funeral. People were lined all away across the city (inaudible).

One of the largest funerals I think outside someone in government or something Baltimore ever had. (Inaudible). And just before the funeral was over, people were all on the rooftops, all around the church.
Blocks away, people just standing on the rooftops looking down. You couldn't get near the church for the people in the street.
And I always said this was a shower of blessing. Before the funeral -- you know, before they brought the body out, it rained like cats and dogs. The rain just came down.
And just about two or three minutes before the funeral was over, it stopped. Nobody moved,
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

moved, just because (inaudible) it was raining, people didn't move from the rooftops, (inaudible) people just stayed in the rain. And we came out, (inaudible) we got flowers en route to the cemetery. (inaudible). So I always say that was a shower of blessing from heaven.
Because it rained so hard for just a few minutes. Nobody know that (inaudible) it was gonna rain. I don't know where the rain came from. It was a nice day. (Inaudible) rain.
You know, the sun was shining and everything. All of sudden this rainstorm come up, passed over a few minutes.
And we stayed there in Baltimore after the funeral for about a couple of days, and then we came back to New York.
